properties.state: {"concern":"core","designation":"internal","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"A second revision of a node in one epoch must not overwrite the first snapshot","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"req:intent-preserved says the past is never overwritten. Snapshot identity currently breaks that rule whenever a node is revised TWICE within a single epoch, and the loss is silent.\\n\\nOBSERVED 2026-07-28, by doing it rather than by reading the code. req:build-loop-is-bounded was amended once (chg:iteration-budget-was-elicited, correcting the iteration budget to an elicited value) and later the same day amended again (chg:build-loop-shape-reassessed, demoting the hard stop). Both used record_change against the same epoch:reflow-workflow-review. The snapshot id is deterministic per (epoch, node) — snap:epoch:reflow-workflow-review:req:build-loop-is-bounded — so the SECOND record_change wrote over the first. compare_designs reported it under supporting.changed with base = the original statement and other = the first-amended statement: the snapshot now holds the INTERMEDIATE state, and the state the node held before any amendment survives only in git, in an export committed earlier.\\n\\nWHY THIS IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY BUG. Nothing failed and nothing warned. record_change returned a prior_snapshot both times and looked identical from the caller's side. The design's own history simply lost a version while reporting success, which is precisely the silent-overwrite failure the revise-design discipline exists to prevent — and the discipline was followed exactly. A user doing careful work by the documented procedure loses history and is never told.\\n\\nIT ALSO BREAKS THE STATED TEST OF A GOOD REVISION. The revise-design skill ends with it: \\\"afterwards, someone reading the graph can answer what did this say before, when did it change, and why — without git archaeology.\\\" After two amendments in one epoch that is false: answering it for the first amendment requires git archaeology, which is the exact fallback the skill promises to remove.\\n\\nTHE SHAPE OF THE FIX IS A CHOICE, and none of the options is obviously right, which is why this is recorded rather than patched. (a) Make snapshot identity per REVISION rather than per (epoch, node) — e.g. include the ChangeEvent id, which is already unique per revision — so every record_change mints a distinct snapshot and HAS_SNAPSHOT becomes one-to-many. Truest to req:intent-preserved; grows the graph faster and makes \\\"the snapshot for this epoch\\\" ambiguous where readers currently assume one. (b) REFUSE a second record_change against the same node in the same epoch, directing the caller to open a new epoch. Cheap and loud, and it forces epoch hygiene, but epochs are meant to bound a round of WORK, not a single edit, so this pushes an unrelated concern onto the caller. (c) Keep one snapshot per epoch deliberately, meaning it holds the state at the START of the epoch, and make the second call a no-op rather than an overwrite. Preserves the original, loses the intermediate, and needs the semantics stated somewhere they are currently only implied.\\n\\nWhichever is chosen, the silence is not defensible: if a revision cannot be snapshotted without discarding an earlier one, the call must say so. Found 2026-07-28 while amending requirements from the reflow workflow review; the amendments themselves are the evidence.","status":"proposed"}
